data.content:
User revisiting this plan with a much broader vision. The original concept of "plan rules in config" has evolved into "Catalysts" - composable, layerable collections of resources that affect questions asked, processes followed, and outputs expected during plan creation.

Key points from the conversation:
- Plans don't have to be about code. Could be about balancing a checkbook, writing a news article, managing finances.
- Amazon-style working backwards: a plan could produce a press release / 6-pager justification document as output. An "Amazon catalyst" would bring those output expectations and prompts.
- Catalysts are domain-specific: front-end development has different assumptions than back-end. Node.js projects differ from Python projects. Tech differs from finance.
- Catalysts can be layered: a base "software" catalyst, then a more specific "Node.js" catalyst on top, or an "Amazon culture" catalyst layered with a "backend services" catalyst.
- Catalysts are guidance, not dictation. They provide guardrails that help people identify areas that need addressing, ask better questions, and ensure key perspectives aren't missed.
- Plans can be strategic or tactical - from long-term vision to small feature work to personal finance.
- Vision: open source repository of industry-specific catalysts that anyone can use, contribute to, and customize.
- User sees this as a potentially huge idea - "a startup to make a billion trillion dollars" (enthusiastic but also grounded - wants to nurture alongside current role).

A Catalyst is defined as: "a collection of resources that is used to help affect the questions that are asked and the process that is used to come up with a plan."

You can:
- Create your own customized catalysts
- Layer catalysts upon each other
- Use them to help guide employees/teams to think about the right topics
- They're about empowerment and culture, not micromanagement
data.context: User revisiting the global-riotplan-rules plan with a much expanded vision around Catalysts concept, from a driving conversation transcript
data.speaker: user

data.note: Evolution: "plan rules" concept has grown into "Catalysts" - composable, layerable guidance packages that shape the entire planning process, not just validation checks. This fundamentally changes scope from config arrays to a pluggable system.

Catalyst definition: "a collection of resources that affects the questions asked and the process used to come up with a plan." Not dictation - guidance. Guardrails that help identify areas needing attention.

Catalyst layering: catalysts stack. Base "software" catalyst + "Node.js" catalyst + "company X culture" catalyst. Each layer adds domain-specific questions, constraints, output expectations, and institutional knowledge.
Catalyst scope is broader than tech: could have catalysts for personal finance planning, blog post creation, news summaries, strategic business planning - any domain where structured thinking helps.

Amazon press release analogy: a catalyst could define expected outputs like a 6-pager or press release. "Install the Amazon catalyst and you get the prompts and content to design the outputs you'd create at Amazon." Output templates are part of what a catalyst provides.
Open source vision: an open repository of industry-specific catalysts that anyone can use, contribute to, and customize. Community-driven domain expertise.

data.content:
User providing detailed examples across all catalyst facets:

QUESTIONS:
- Node.js catalyst: What version? What dependencies? Publish to NPMJS or GitHub?
- Finance catalyst: Look at spending in certain areas, seasonal considerations like Christmas
- Questions aren't hyper-specific, they provide general overall guidance about things that need to be known to support the catalyst's domain area

CONSTRAINTS:
- Don't have to be domain-specific. Can be universal across all plans.
- Example: All plans must have a step focused on tests, a step focused on documentation
- Documentation steps must focus on README.md, the website, and the AI guide
- These are the kind of baseline expectations you set once

OUTPUT TEMPLATES / DELIVERABLES:
- Need to add concept of an "output directory" to a plan (had a plan yesterday that generated blog posts, put them in root directory - would love an output/ directory)
- Expected deliverables: produce a press release for the feature, produce a 6-page narrative document (Amazon style)
- When creating a plan, you're also creating a proposal to get the plan approved

DOMAIN KNOWLEDGE:
- Like rules but also general things you need to know about the organization or the project
- Institutional knowledge, context about how things work

PROCESS GUIDANCE:
- Would be very interesting to shape HOW the planning process itself works

WHERE IN LIFECYCLE:
- Everywhere. The catalyst's inputs - guidance, templates, domain knowledge - affect every part of the lifecycle
- There's a baseline, then catalysts layer on influence
- Catalysts can be applied in an order

AUDIENCE / DIMENSIONS:
- Technology catalysts: Java, Node, Ruby
- Domain catalysts: finance, technology, legal
- Project catalysts: specific to individual projects
- Organization catalysts: for an org like Kjerneverk or Redaction
- Personal catalysts: across all projects a person works on
- These are somewhat orthogonal dimensions - you apply a COMBINATION of catalysts
- Some could be incompatible - that's where it gets interesting

FIRST CATALYST:
- For Kjerneverk/Redaction projects: every plan needs rigorous testing step, rigorous documentation step
- If creating a new project: ensure GitHub infrastructure, all tests are set up
- Could go up a level: a catalyst for ALL projects across ALL organizations

data.speaker: user

data.note: Catalyst dimensions are orthogonal planes: Technology (Java, Node, Ruby), Domain (finance, legal, tech), Project (specific repo), Organization (Kjerneverk, Redaction), Personal (across everything). You apply a combination. Some may be incompatible.
New feature need: plans should have an "output directory" concept. Generated artifacts (blog posts, press releases, 6-pagers) should go in an output/ directory, not the plan root.
Catalyst questions aren't hyper-specific interrogation -- they're general guidance about "things that need to be known" to support the catalyst's domain. They shape the conversation, not dictate it.

Plans as proposals: when creating a plan with output templates (press release, 6-pager), the plan itself becomes a proposal that needs approval. The catalyst shapes both the plan AND the artifacts that justify it.

data.constraint: Catalysts must be composable -- multiple catalysts applied together in a defined order, with their influence layering on top of a baseline
Catalysts must affect the entire lifecycle -- idea exploration, shaping, plan generation, validation, feedback -- not just one phase
Catalyst system must support multiple orthogonal dimensions: technology, domain, project, organization, personal -- without forcing a single taxonomy

User answering how RiotPlan knows which catalysts to use, and what metadata catalysts carry:

HOW CATALYSTS ARE SELECTED:
- Config-based (riotplan config lists default catalysts)
- Command-line (pass catalyst when creating a plan)
- MCP: add ability to list available catalysts, and associate a plan with a catalyst through the MCP
- If config-based, everything automatically gets covered by the configured catalysts

PLANS NEED A YAML FILE:

- Catalyst configuration can be stored there (but don't worry about catalyst config details yet)

- Name
- Description
- Version (the NPM version)
- Which facets are provided, plus some configuration
- Don't want to get into taxonomy of catalysts yet -- keep it simple for now

- Catalyst taxonomy/typing
- Incompatibility handling

data.name: NPM-Distributed Catalyst Packages
data.description: Catalysts are NPM packages containing a directory structure with a catalyst.yml manifest and facet content (questions, constraints, output templates, domain knowledge, process guidance, validation rules). Plans gain a plan.yaml manifest that records title, ID, and associated catalyst IDs. RiotPlan resolves catalysts from node_modules, merges their facets in declared order, and injects the merged content into the appropriate lifecycle phases (idea exploration, shaping, plan generation, validation, feedback). Three selection channels: project config (defaults), CLI flags, and MCP tools. Implementation requires: 1) Define catalyst package structure and manifest schema, 2) Add plan.yaml manifest to plans, 3) Build catalyst resolution/loading from node_modules, 4) Build facet merging logic (ordered layering), 5) Inject merged content into generator prompts, 6) Add MCP tools for catalyst listing and plan-catalyst association, 7) Add traceability (catalysts used recorded in plan output).
tradeoffs: Leverages NPM ecosystem for versioning, distribution, and dependency management -- no custom registry needed
Directory-based structure with YAML manifest is simple to author and inspect
Facet-based architecture (questions, constraints, templates, knowledge, guidance, validation) keeps concerns separated
Layered composition with ordered merging gives predictable behavior
Requires plan.yaml -- new infrastructure that changes plan structure
NPM dependency means catalysts must be installed before use -- no ad-hoc loading from URLs or paths (npm link covers local dev)
Complexity: touches every lifecycle phase (exploration, shaping, generation, validation, feedback, MCP)
Defers incompatibility detection, catalyst taxonomy, and catalyst configuration for later
assumptions: Catalysts are authored infrequently and consumed often -- authoring complexity is acceptable
NPM is the right distribution channel for the target audience
Ordered layering (last catalyst wins on conflicts) is sufficient merge strategy for v1
The six facets identified (questions, constraints, output templates, domain knowledge, process guidance, validation rules) are the right decomposition
Plan YAML manifest is a welcome addition to plan infrastructure, not disruptive

data.name: Foundation-First: Catalyst Internals Then NPM Distribution
data.description: Same end-state as NPM-Distributed Catalyst Packages, but phased differently. Phase 1: Build the catalyst engine internally -- define the catalyst schema, facet loading, merging, and injection into lifecycle phases. Catalysts in Phase 1 are just local directories (no NPM). The plan.yaml manifest is added. Config-based catalyst selection works by pointing to local directories. Phase 2: Add NPM package resolution so catalysts can be installed as dependencies. Phase 3: Add MCP tools for catalyst listing and association. This approach separates the core concept (what is a catalyst, how does it influence plans) from the distribution mechanism (NPM) and the interface (MCP).
tradeoffs: Reduces initial scope -- can ship catalyst support without NPM packaging infrastructure
Allows rapid iteration on catalyst schema and facet structure before locking it into published packages
Local-directory catalysts are easier to author and test during development
More incremental -- each phase delivers value independently
Takes longer to reach the full vision of shared/published catalysts
Risk of building local-only features that don't translate well to NPM distribution later
Three phases means three rounds of integration work instead of one cohesive push
assumptions: The catalyst schema will need iteration -- better to iterate locally before publishing
Local directory catalysts provide enough value to be worth shipping as an intermediate step
NPM distribution can be cleanly layered on top of local resolution without refactoring
MCP integration is separable from core catalyst functionality

data.content:
User selecting Foundation-First approach and raising an important architectural question: should catalyst implementation live in the main riotplan codebase, or in a separate, simpler module?

Reasoning: if you're going to implement catalysts, the full riotplan source code is complex. A separate module would be simpler to work with, easier to test, and cleaner to reason about. Possibly a "riotplan-catalyst" or similar package that handles catalyst loading, resolution, merging, and schema -- consumed by riotplan as a dependency.

This aligns with the monorepo/multi-package approach already in use (execution, execution-anthropic, execution-gemini, etc.).

data.note: Architecture decision: catalysts likely need their own package (e.g. @kjerneverk/catalyst or @kjerneverk/riotplan-catalyst). This follows the existing pattern -- execution, execution-anthropic, agentic, riotprompt are all separate repos/packages consumed by riotplan. A catalyst package would handle schema, loading, resolution, merging -- riotplan consumes it.
